# Major neurocognitive disorder

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Neurocognitive disorders > Major neurocognitive disorder*

[Original Article Link](/library/v30A4f)

---

## Summary

Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia) is an acquired disorder of cognitive function that is commonly characterized by impairments in the <u>memory</u>, language, attention, <u>executive function</u>, <u>social cognition</u>, and/or <u>perceptual-motor</u> domains. Most forms are associated with older age. The most common <u>causes of dementia</u> are neurodegenerative (e.g., <u>Alzheimer disease</u>) and vascular disease. While all <u>subtypes of dementia</u> share impairments in <u>cognition</u>, other clinical features may differ depending on the <u>dementia subtype</u>. Initial diagnosis should focus on <u>patient history</u> and <u>neurological examination</u>, including a <u>cognitive assessment</u>. Additional laboratory tests and <u>neuroimaging</u> studies are often necessary to investigate specific causes. An important differential diagnosis is <u>pseudodementia</u>. In contrast to patients with dementia, individuals with <u>pseudodementia</u> often recall the onset of their cognitive impairments, overestimate their symptoms, and are responsive to treatment with <u>antidepressants</u>. In general, specific pharmacotherapy to slow the loss of cognitive function in dementia is of modest benefit; management should focus on nonpharmacological measures. Preventive interventions to reduce <u>modifiable risk factors</u> for dementia (e.g., control of <u>ASCVD risk factors</u>, <u>treatment of hearing loss</u>) may help prevent or slow cognitive decline, although studies assessing the <u>efficacy</u> of specific interventions are lacking. There are no universal <u>screening recommendations</u> for dementia, but clinicians should be vigilant for early signs of cognitive decline in all individuals to allow for early management, e.g., management of reversible causes, adjustment of other medical treatments.

---

## Etiology

### Neurodegenerative brain diseases




* <u>Alzheimer disease</u> (> 50% of dementia cases)

* <u>Parkinson disease</u>

* <u>Frontotemporal dementia</u>

* <u>Dementia with Lewy bodies</u>

* <u>Progressive supranuclear palsy</u>

* <u>Huntington disease</u>





### Additional causes




* <u>Cerebrovascular disease</u> (20% of dementia cases)

* Multi-<u>infarct</u> dementia

* Diffuse <u>white matter</u> disease (<u>subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy</u>)

* <u>Hypoxic</u> <u>brain damage</u>

* <u>Normal pressure hydrocephalus</u>

* After <u>head trauma</u>, <u>intracranial bleeding</u> or <u>brain tumors</u>

* Drug/alcohol‑related (e.g., Wernicke‑Korsakoff syndrome)

* <u>Wilson disease</u>

* <u>Vitamin deficiencies</u> (<u>thiamine</u>, B<sub>6</sub>, B<sub>12</sub>, <u>folate</u>, <u>niacin</u>)

* Metabolic: <u>exsiccosis</u>, <u>uremia</u>, <u>electrolyte</u> imbalances

* Endocrine: <u>hypothyroidism</u> and <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>hypoparathyroidism</u> and <u>hyperparathyroidism</u>

* Environmental toxins

* Inflammatory/infectious

* <u>Syphilis</u>

* <u>Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy</u>

* <u>HIV</u>

* <u>Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Think DEMENTIAS for common etiologies of dementia: Degenerative (Alzheimer, Parkinson, <u>frontotemporal dementia</u>), Emotional (<u>depression</u>, <u>psychosis</u>), Metabolic (<u>liver</u> or <u>kidney failure</u>, toxins), Endocrine (<u>hypothyroidism</u>), Nutritional (<u>vitamin deficiencies</u>) or Neoplastic (<u>carcinomatous meningitis</u>), Traumatic (<u>TBI</u>), Infectious (<u>syphilis</u>, <u>HIV</u>, <u>CJD</u>), Autoimmune, Stroke.




References:[[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

---

## Clinical features

* General: <u>memory</u> impairment

* Additional cognitive impairment

* Speech: <u>aphasia</u>, word-finding difficulties, semantic paraphasia

* Intellectual capacities, reasoning, planning capabilities, and self-control

* Spatial-temporal awareness (however, the awareness of oneself remains stable for a long time)

* <u>Apathy</u>

* Changes in <u>personality</u>, mood, and behavior

* Early stages: <u>depression</u>

* Later stages: seemingly unconcerned mood and cognitive impairment is downplayed

* Dementia associated with <u>CNS</u> infections

* Most types of <u>CNS</u> infections cause acute neurological or psychiatric symptoms rather than dementia.

* Infections that may cause <u>symptoms of dementia</u> include:

* <u>Chronic meningitis</u>

* <u>HIV</u> and <u>HIV</u>-related <u>opportunistic infections</u>

* <u>Neurosyphilis</u>





References:[[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[2]](/library/uDcpTe0)[[3]](/library/9DcNge0)




* Perform a comprehensive clinical evaluation, including:

* Detailed history of cognitive decline

* Evaluation for <u>risk factors</u> for and/or symptoms of specific <u>types of dementia</u>

* <u>Neurological examination</u>, including a <u>mental status examination</u> and <u>cognitive assessment</u>

* Assess for reversible causes of cognitive impairment, including;  <u>delirium</u> and <u>pseudodementia</u>.

* See “<u>Delirium vs. dementia</u>.”

* <u>Review medications</u> on the <u>Beers Criteria</u>.

* Screen for <u>major depressive disorder</u> using <u>PHQ-2</u>.

* Confirm the diagnosis using <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria for neurocognitive disorders.

* Obtain laboratory tests and <u>neuroimaging</u> to assess for underlying <u>causes of major neurocognitive disorder</u>.

* Refer patients with <u>early-onset dementia</u>, <u>rapidly progressive dementia</u>, or if more information is needed to guide management.

* <u>Neurology</u>: specialized testing, including <u>neuroimaging</u>, <u>CSF</u> evaluation, <u>EEG</u>, or <u>genetic testing</u>

* Geriatric <u>psychiatry</u>: full <u>neuropsychological testing</u>





> [!TIP]
> The <u>USPSTF</u> has found insufficient evidence for or against screening for cognitive impairment in individuals with no symptoms; however, assessment for cognitive impairment is a routine part of the <u>Medicare</u> <u>Annual Wellness Visit</u>. [[4]](/library/LDcwUe0)




### Diagnostic criteria for neurocognitive disorders [[2]](/library/uDcpTe0)[[5]](/library/MDcMUe0)[[6]](/library/De11aT0)




#### <u>Diagnostic criteria for major neurocognitive disorder</u> (dementia)




These criteria are in accordance with <u>DSM-5</u>. Unlike <u>DSM-5</u>, <u>ICD</u>-10 includes <u>memory</u> impairment as a diagnostic criterion.




| <br><u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria for major neurocognitive disorder (dementia) [[2]](/library/uDcpTe0)[[5]](/library/MDcMUe0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Decline in ≥ 1 domain | <br><br>* <u>Learning and memory</u>, including registration (<u>immediate memory</u>) and recall (<u>short-term memory</u>)<br><br>* Language, including object naming, word-finding, fluency, grammar, and semantics<br><br>* <u>Executive function</u><br><br>* <u>Complex attention</u><br><br>* <u>Perceptual-motor</u><br><br>* <u>Social cognition</u><br><br><br> |
| Additional requirements | <br><br>* Evidence of decline confirmed by both:<br><br>* The patient, a knowledgeable source, or the clinician<br><br>* Impaired performance on <u>neuropsychological testing</u> or other <u>cognitive assessments</u><br><br>* Cognitive deficits interfere with everyday life.<br><br>* Not better explained by another disorder (e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u>)<br><br>* Deficits do not occur exclusively in the context of <u>delirium</u>.<br><br><br> |
| Severity | <br><br>* Mild: difficulties with <u>instrumental activities of daily living</u> (<u>IADLs</u>)<br><br>* Moderate: difficulties with <u>basic activities of daily living</u> (<u>basic ADLs</u>)<br><br>* Severe: Patients are fully dependent.<br><br><br> |





#### Diagnostic criteria for mild neurocognitive disorder (<u>mild cognitive impairment</u>)




Diagnostic criteria are similar to dementia, with the following differences:




* Cognitive deficits are less severe, i.e., do not interfere with everyday life.

* Patients are typically aware of their deficits.





> [!TIP]
> The defining difference between <u>MCI</u> and dementia is the degree of functional impairment and cognitive decline.




### Initial evaluation of major neurocognitive disorder [[2]](/library/uDcpTe0)[[3]](/library/9DcNge0)




Obtain the following studies in all patients with suspected dementia to identify the cause of dementia and/or rule out other causes (e.g., <u>delirium</u>).




* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>Vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u> (<u>cobalamin</u>): assess for deficiency

* <u>TSH</u>: <u>hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>anemia</u>

* <u>CMP</u>: <u>kidney</u> disease, <u>liver</u> disease, and <u>hypoglycemia</u> or <u>hyperglycemia</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>: rule out infection

* Imaging [[2]](/library/uDcpTe0)[[7]](/library/wDchge0)[[8]](/library/tb1Xv20)[[9]](/library/511ihf0)

* <u>Brain</u> <u>MRI</u> is the preferred modality.

* Obtain to detect reversible or structural <u>causes of dementia</u>.

* Findings depend on the underlying disease and frequently include cortical <u>atrophy</u>.

* See “<u>Differential diagnosis of subtypes of dementia</u>” for a comparison of imaging findings.





![Comparison of MRI images in healthy control, Alzheimer disease, and vascular dementia](media/lq9m1e72wonu7qcuvhm529z8.jpg)

Comparison of MRI images in healthy control, Alzheimer disease, and vascular dementia




### Additional studies [[2]](/library/uDcpTe0)[[10]](/library/nwc7je0)




Obtain as indicated under specialist guidance in patients with a rapidly progressive course of dementia, early-onset dementia (< 65 years), or symptoms, <u>risk factors</u>, or other findings suggestive of a specific type of dementia.




* Blood tests

* <u>CBC with differential</u>

* <u>Folate</u> (<u>vitamin B<sub>9</sub></u>) and <u>homocysteine</u>: ↓ <u>folate</u> and ↑ <u>homocysteine</u> associated with cognitive impairment  [[11]](/library/MwcMje0)

* <u>ESR</u>, <u>CRP</u>, <u>ANA</u>: inflammatory or autoimmune diseases

* <u>RPR</u>: if there is clinical suspicion for <u>neurosyphilis</u>

* Lyme <u>titers</u>: if there is clinical suspicion for <u>chronic neuroborreliosis</u>

* <u>HIV screening</u>: to rule out <u>HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder</u>

* <u>Ceruloplasmin</u>: to rule out <u>Wilson disease</u>

* <u>Urine toxicology screen</u>

* <u>Lumbar puncture</u> to: [[10]](/library/nwc7je0)

* Assess for evidence of <u>CNS</u> inflammation (e.g., <u>meningitis</u>, <u>encephalitis</u>) or <u>prion disease</u>

* Detect specific biomarkers (e.g., in <u>Alzheimer disease</u>)

* Confirm <u>normal pressure hydrocephalus</u> (<u>CSF tap test</u>)

* <u>PET scan</u> or <u>SPECT</u>: to distinguish between specific <u>neurodegenerative disorders</u>

* <u>Electroencephalogram</u> (<u>EEG</u>): to evaluate for <u>seizures</u>, subcortical dementia, and <u>frontal lobe</u> degeneration [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[12]](/library/xDcEge0)

## Cognitive assessment

### General principles [[2]](/library/uDcpTe0)[[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[13]](/library/KDcU2e0)[[14]](/library/8wcOke0)




* Shorter screening tools (e.g., <u>Mini-Cog</u>) have adequate <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u> for detecting dementia in most situations.

* Utilize a more extensive screening tool (e.g., <u>Mini-Mental State Examination</u> or <u>Montreal Cognitive Assessment</u>):

* For diagnostic clarity

* To assess the degree of cognitive impairment (e.g., <u>MMSE</u> < 24 suggests cognitive impairment)

* Factors such as education level, language, and illness can impact results.

* Repeat measurements to track disease progression over time.

* See “<u>Mental status examination</u>” for further details on cognitive domains.





> [!TIP]
> Obtain <u>neuropsychological testing</u> if there is diagnostic uncertainty despite the use of extensive screening tools.




### <u>Overview of cognitive screening tools</u>




| <br>Overview of cognitive screening tools<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time requirement | Test | Domains assessed | Important considerations |
| < 5 minutes | <br>Clock-drawing test  [[15]](/library/GwcB4e0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Complex attention</u><br><br>* <u>Executive function</u><br><br>* <u>Perceptual-motor</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Free for general use<br><br>* Commonly used as part of or in combination with other screening tools<br><br><br> |
| <br>Memory Impairment Screen (<u>MIS</u>) [[16]](/library/L11whf0)<br> | <br>* <u>Learning and memory</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Free for general use<br><br>* Scoring<br><br>* Range: 0–8<br><br>* ≤ 4 suggests cognitive impairment<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Mini-Cog  [[17]](/library/6Dcj2e0)[[18]](/library/pDcL2e0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Complex attention</u><br><br>* <u>Executive function</u><br><br>* <u>Learning and memory</u><br><br>* <u>Perceptual-motor</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Free for general use<br><br>* Reliable results across ethnolinguistically diverse populations<br><br>* Scoring<br><br>* Range: 0–5<br><br>* < 3 suggests cognitive impairment<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Six-item screener (<u>SIS</u>) [[19]](/library/o1103f0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Learning and memory</u><br><br>* <u>Orientation to person, place, and time</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Free for general use<br><br>* Scoring<br><br>* Range: 0–6<br><br>* ≤ 4 suggests cognitive impairment<br><br><br> |  |
| 5–15 minutes | <br>Mini Mental State Examination (<u>MMSE</u>)  [[20]](/library/-b1Dw20)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Complex attention</u><br><br>* Language<br><br>* <u>Learning and memory</u><br><br>* <u>Orientation to person, place, and time</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Proprietary test; requires a fee for use<br><br>* Considered easier than <u>MoCA</u><br><br>* Scoring<br><br>* Range: 0–30<br><br>* < 24 suggests cognitive impairment<br><br><br> |
| <br>Montreal Cognitive Assessment (<u>MoCA</u>) [[21]](/library/twcXke0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Complex attention</u><br><br>* <u>Executive function</u><br><br>* Language<br><br>* <u>Learning and memory</u><br><br>* <u>Orientation to person, place, and time</u><br><br>* <u>Perceptual-motor</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* One-hour training and certification are required before use.<br><br>* Distinguishes between <u>MCI</u> and dementia better than <u>MMSE</u><br><br>* May be too difficult for patients with advanced dementia<br><br>* Scoring<br><br>* Range: 0–30<br><br>* < 26 suggests cognitive impairment<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Saint Louis University Mental Status Examination (<u>SLUMS</u>) [[22]](/library/HwcK4e0)<br> | <br><br>* Free for general use<br><br>* More sensitive than <u>MMSE</u>, especially for detecting <u>MCI</u><br><br>* Accounts for level of education<br><br>* Scoring<br><br>* Range: 0–30<br><br>* < 27 suggests cognitive impairment<br><br><br> |  |  |

## Differential diagnoses

| <br>Differential diagnosis of subtypes of dementia [[23]](/library/LgYwDo) |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Course of disease | Distinctive clinical features | Studies & imaging | Pathology |
| Normal <u>aging</u> | <br>* Insidious onset, typically starting in the sixth/seventh decade<br><br> | <br><br>* Mild decline in some cognitive areas → episodic and <u>working memory</u> affected first<br><br>* Procedural and <u>semantic memory</u> typically preserved<br><br>* Independence in daily activities is preserved<br><br><br> | <br>* No specific tests available<br><br> | <br>* General loss of <u>brain</u> volume (<u>white matter</u> more affected than <u>gray matter</u>)<br><br> |
| <br>Pseudodementia [[24]](/library/oia0s4) | <br><br>* Associated with major <u>depression</u>, especially in elderly patients<br><br>* Cognitive deficits typically manifest after mood symptoms<br><br>* Typically sudden onset<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Mimics dementia<br><br>* Complaints of <u>memory</u> loss<br><br>* Mostly <u>depressed mood</u><br><br>* Patients are able to recall onset of symptoms.<br><br>* Patient gives short answers, e.g., “I don't know”<br><br>* <u>Cognition</u> usually improves after effective <u>antidepressant</u> therapy.<br><br><br> | <br>* No specific tests available<br><br> | <br>* Structural or metabolic abnormalities that are associated with <u>depression</u> (e.g., lesions of the <u>limbic system</u>)<br><br> |
| <u>Alzheimer disease</u> (AD) | <br>* Slowly progressive, over ∼ 8–10 years<br><br> | <br><br>* Episodic impairment of <u>memory</u><br><br>* Characteristic order of language impairment: naming → comprehension → fluency<br><br><br> | <br><br>* AD is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u><br><br>* <u>MRI</u>   <br><br>* Diffuse cortical <u>atrophy</u><br><br>* Hippocampal <u>atrophy</u><br><br>* <u>CSF</u><br><br>* ↓ Beta <u>amyloid</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Phosphorylated</u> <u>tau</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Neuritic plaques</u> (<u>amyloid beta</u> <u>peptides</u>, mainly accumulating extracellularly)<br><br>* <u>Neurofibrillary tangles</u> (abnormally <u>phosphorylated</u> <u>tau</u> protein, which accumulates intracellularly)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Vascular dementia</u> (VD) | <br>* May present with abrupt cognitive decline and stepwise deterioration<br><br> | <br>* Asymmetric or focal deficits (e.g., <u>hemiparesis</u>)<br><br> | <br>* CT/<u>MRI</u>: multiple cortical and <u>lacunar infarcts</u>, <u>white matter</u> lesions  [[25]](/library/ELX8zA)<br><br> |  |
| <u>Dementia with Lewy bodies</u> (<u>DLB</u>) | <br>* Steady decline; typically over ∼ 8–10 years but more rapid progression is possible<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Visual hallucinations</u> and parkinsonian motor disorders<br><br>* Attention impairment<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>MRI</u><br><br>* Diffuse mild cortical <u>atrophy</u><br><br>* <u>Atrophy</u> of <u>substantia innominata</u> and mesopontine <u>gray matter</u> [[26]](/library/OLXIBA)<br><br>* <u>SPECT</u>: may reveal decreased occipital <u>perfusion</u>/metabolism<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lewy bodies</u> (intracellular aggregations of mainly <u>α-Synuclein</u>)<br><br> |
| <u>Frontotemporal dementia</u> (<u>FTD</u>) | <br>* Usually manifests between ages 40–69<br><br> | <br>* <u>Behavioral variant FTD</u> (most common) → early changes in <u>personality</u>, <u>apathy</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>CSF</u>: usually normal or ↑ <u>Aβ</u> 1–42<br><br>* PET or <u>SPECT</u> to reveal metabolic disorders in the frontal and <u>temporal lobes</u><br><br>* <u>MRI</u>: <u>atrophy</u> of the frontal and/or <u>temporal lobes</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Focal cortical <u>atrophy</u><br><br> |
| <u>Normal pressure hydrocephalus</u> (<u>NPH</u>) | <br>* Potentially reversible<br><br> | <br>* Classic clinical triad<br><br>* Gait disorder<br><br>* Dementia<br><br>* <u>Urinary incontinence</u><br><br> | <br><br>* CT/<u>MRI</u>: relative dilatation of ventricles with periventricular hyperintensities<br><br>* <u>Lumbar puncture</u> alleviates symptoms<br><br><br> | <br>* Unspecific <u>cerebral atrophy</u><br><br> |
| Parkinson | <br>* Cognitive impairment develops in advanced disease<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Bradykinesia</u><br><br>* <u>Resting tremor</u><br><br>* Rigidity<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u><br><br>* <u>MRI</u>: <u>atrophy</u> of the cortex, <u>hippocampus</u>, <u>amygdala</u> [[27]](/library/Gb1BE20)<br><br><br> | <br>* Progressive <u>dopaminergic</u> <u>neuron</u> degeneration in the <u>substantia nigra</u> (part of the <u>basal ganglia</u>) and the <u>locus coeruleus</u><br><br> |
| <u>Wernicke encephalopathy</u> (WE) and <u>Wernicke-Korsakoff</u> syndrome (<u>WKS</u>) | <br>* Potentially reversible<br><br> | <br><br>* WE (classic clinical triad)<br><br>* Confusion<br><br>* <u>Ataxia</u><br><br>* <u>Ophthalmoplegia</u><br><br>* <u>WKS</u><br><br>* Severe anterograde and <u>retrograde amnesia</u>, <u>apathy</u>, confusion, <u>anosognosia</u><br><br>* Other cognitive capacities remain comparatively intact.<br><br><br> | <br>* No specific laboratory test or imaging study is available to definitively rule out <u>Wernicke encephalopathy</u> or <u>Wernicke-Korsakoff</u> syndrome<br><br> | <br><br>* Acute WE: <u>gliosis</u>, inflammation, and/or <u>necrosis</u>, particularly in periventricular structures (e.g., the <u>medial</u> <u>thalamus</u>)<br><br>* Chronic WE/<u>WKS</u>: <u>atrophy</u> of the mamillary bodies<br><br><br> |
| Late <u>neurosyphilis</u> | <br>* Progresses many years after primary infection (∼ 20 years)<br><br> | <br><br>* Signs of late <u>neurosyphilis</u> include:<br><br>* <u>Frontotemporal dementia</u>, <u>psychosis</u>, cognitive dysfunction, <u>personality</u> changes<br><br>* <u>Paresis</u><br><br>* <u>Argyll Robertson pupil</u><br><br>* <u>Tabes dorsalis</u><br><br>* Possibly other signs of <u>tertiary syphilis</u>, including:<br><br>* <u>Gumma</u><br><br>* <u>Cardiovascular syphilis</u><br><br>* May have history of primary or <u>secondary syphilis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Positive (screening) <u>nontreponemal tests</u> (e.g., <u>RPR</u>, <u>VDRL</u>)<br><br>* Positive (confirmatory) <u>treponemal tests</u> (e.g., <u>TPPA</u>, <u>FTA-ABS</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* Direct detection possible via <u>darkfield microscopy</u><br><br> |
| <u>Wilson disease</u> | <br>* Begins with subclinical <u>hepatitis</u> and progresses to <u>liver cirrhosis</u> and neuropsychiatric involvement if left untreated<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Liver</u> disease<br><br>* <u>Kayser-Fleischer rings</u><br><br>* Extrapyramidal motor disturbances (e.g., <u>parkinsonism</u>, <u>tremor</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Slit lamp examination</u><br><br>* ↑ Free serum <u>copper</u>, ↓ serum <u>ceruloplasmin</u><br><br>* <u>MRI</u>: hyperintensities in the <u>putamen</u>, <u>thalamus</u>, and <u>brain stem</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Copper</u> accumulation in the <u>putamen</u>, <u>thalamus</u>, and <u>brain stem</u><br><br> |
| <br><u>Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy</u> (e.g., in <u>AIDS</u>) | <br>* Symptoms due to <u>PML</u> are insidious in onset and can progress over several weeks<br><br> | <br>* <u>Focal neurologic deficits</u>: e.g., <u>hemiplegia</u>, <u>aphasia</u>, <u>ataxia</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>MRI</u>: multifocal, bilateral, asymmetric <u>white matter</u> lesions without <u>mass effect</u> (frontal, parietal and occipital lobes are mostly commonly involved)<br><br>* <u>CSF</u> <u>PCR</u> for detection of <u>JC virus</u> <u>DNA</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Demyelination</u> of <u>axons</u>, enlarged <u>oligodendrocyte</u> <u>nuclei</u> with intranuclear <u>inclusions</u>, bizarre <u>astrocytes</u><br><br> |
| <u>Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease</u> | <br>* <u>Rapidly progressive dementia</u> (weeks to months)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Myoclonus</u> triggered by startling (e.g., loud noises)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>CSF</u>: presence of <u>14-3-3 protein</u><br><br>* <u>EEG</u>: triphasic <u>periodic sharp wave complexes</u> with a frequency of 1–2 Hz<br><br>* <u>MRI</u>: hyperintensities in the <u>basal ganglia</u>, <u>insular cortices</u>, and the frontal cortices<br><br><br> | <br>* Spongiform degeneration (e.g., intracytoplasmic <u>vacuoles</u> within the <u>neurons</u> of cerebral and <u>cerebellar cortex</u>), <u>gliosis</u> and, in rare cases, <u>amyloid plaques</u><br><br> |
| <u>Huntington disease</u> | <br>* Steady decline over 15–20 years<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Chorea</u><br><br>* <u>Athetosis</u><br><br>* Psychiatric dysfunction (e.g., <u>depression</u>, <u>psychosis</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Genetic testing</u> for number of CAG repeats<br><br>* CT/<u>MRI</u>: <u>atrophy</u> of the <u>striatum</u>, most pronounced in the <u>caudate nucleus</u> with consequent enlargement of ventricles (<u>ex vacuo ventriculomegaly</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Atrophy</u> of caudate and <u>putamen</u><br><br>* General <u>cerebral atrophy</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Think VITAMINS for the most common causes of <u>rapidly progressive dementia</u>: Vascular, Infectious, Toxic-metabolic, Autoimmune, Metastases, Iatrogenic, Neurodegenerative, Systemic/Seizures/Structural.

## Management

### Approach [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[28]](/library/-DcDSe0)[[29]](/library/6wcjPe0)




* Provide disease-specific treatment if available.

* Initiate supportive management and management of associated conditions.

* Arrange support for patients and their caregivers. [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[30]](/library/nDc7Ue0)[[31]](/library/ZwcZhe0)

* Consider referral to <u>hospice</u> for eligible patients. [[32]](/library/awcQhe0)





> [!TIP]
> Behavioral problems (e.g., physical <u>agitation</u>) and <u>fecal incontinence</u> in patients with dementia are associated with <u>caregiver burnout</u> and poor outcomes for patients (e.g., emergency department visits and institutionalization). [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[29]](/library/6wcjPe0)[[33]](/library/IDcYfe0)




### Pharmacological <u>treatment of dementia</u> [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[28]](/library/-DcDSe0)[[30]](/library/nDc7Ue0)




* <u>Antidementia medications</u> may provide modest benefit for cognitive symptoms in some <u>types of dementia</u>.

* <u>Cholinesterase inhibitors</u> (<u>donepezil</u>, <u>galantamine</u>, <u>rivastigmine</u>)

* Recommended for mild to moderate <u>Alzheimer disease</u>  [[30]](/library/nDc7Ue0)

* May be considered in patients with <u>Parkinson dementia</u> or <u>dementia with Lewy bodies</u>

* Discuss treatment goals and potential adverse effects before starting medication.  [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[30]](/library/nDc7Ue0)[[34]](/library/CS1qbg0)

* Reevaluate patients 12 weeks after initiation. [[34]](/library/CS1qbg0)

* Ensure the benefits outweigh the adverse effects.

* Discontinue if no beneficial cognitive effects are observed.  [[34]](/library/CS1qbg0)[[35]](/library/YfWnkk0)

* <u>NMDA-receptor antagonist</u> (<u>memantine</u>): recommended for moderate to severe <u>Alzheimer disease</u>

* See “<u>Antidementia medications</u>” in “<u>Alzheimer disease</u>” for more information.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Antidementia medications</u> provide limited improvement of cognitive symptoms. Use <u>shared decision-making</u> to determine if pharmacotherapy is appropriate for the patient after discussing the risks, benefits, and alternatives. [[28]](/library/-DcDSe0)[[31]](/library/ZwcZhe0)[[34]](/library/CS1qbg0)




> [!TIP]
> Discontinue <u>cholinesterase inhibitors</u> approximately 12 weeks after initiation if no beneficial cognitive effects are observed. [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[34]](/library/CS1qbg0)




### Supportive management of patients with dementia [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[28]](/library/-DcDSe0)[[31]](/library/ZwcZhe0)




* Regularly evaluate for associated medical, psychiatric, or behavioral conditions.

* Manage <u>risk factors</u> (see “<u>Prevention of dementia</u>”).

* Use <u>delirium prevention</u> strategies.

* Treat <u>hearing loss</u> and <u>vision loss</u> if necessary.

* Periodically perform an <u>assessment of care needs for older adults</u>. [[36]](/library/qDcC2e0)

* Coordinate <u>functional status assessments</u>.

* Offer <u>psychoeducation</u>.

* Assess for <u>caregiver burnout</u> and provide referrals for assistance.

* Encourage early <u>advance care planning</u> and financial planning.

* Recommend maintaining a:

* Predictable schedule

* Familiar home environment

* Encourage a healthy lifestyle, including:

* Exercise

* Recreational activities, e.g., social gatherings, art, puzzles, music, pet therapy

* <u>Mediterranean diet</u>

* <u>Sleep hygiene</u>, including a regular <u>sleep</u> schedule

* Personal hygiene

* Consider cognitive interventions for patients with mild to moderate dementia. [[37]](/library/AeWRYk0)[[38]](/library/rp1fI30)

* <u>Cognitive training</u>: may result in small gains in verbal fluency and <u>global</u> <u>cognition</u> [[39]](/library/G2WBQk0)

* <u>Cognitive stimulation therapy</u>: may improve cognitive function and reduce <u>depression</u> [[40]](/library/t2WXjk0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Cognitive training</u> and <u>cognitive stimulation therapy</u> may modestly delay cognitive decline. However, these programs can lead to excessive frustration, which may exacerbate behavioral and neuropsychiatric symptoms. [[28]](/library/-DcDSe0)[[31]](/library/ZwcZhe0)




> [!TIP]
> Patients with dementia are less likely to receive adequate <u>pain management</u> at the end of life. Consider using a <u>nonverbal pain scale</u> to <u>assess pain</u>, and follow a step-wise approach to <u>analgesia</u>.




#### Safety considerations




* Inform the patient and caregivers about increased risk of driving accidents.

* Consider referral for driving safety evaluation to assess for <u>driving restrictions</u>.

* Consider the need for interventions (e.g., supervision) to prevent wandering.

* Evaluate for risk of <u>falls in older adults</u>.





#### <u>Advance care planning</u> (<u>ACP</u>) [[41]](/library/0wcehe0)




* Discuss <u>ACP</u> at the time of diagnosis, or with changes in health status, residence, or financial situation.

* Document wishes and preferences, including a <u>physician orders for life sustaining treatment</u>, <u>advance directive</u>, and <u>medical power of attorney</u>.

* Consider a specific <u>advance directive</u> for dementia. [[42]](/library/09ceNe0)

* Assess <u>decision-making capacity</u> regularly.





### Management of behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[32]](/library/awcQhe0)




* <u>Major depressive disorder</u> and <u>anxiety</u>: Consider low dose of an <u>SSRI</u> (e.g., <u>escitalopram</u> or <u>citalopram</u>). [[28]](/library/-DcDSe0)[[31]](/library/ZwcZhe0)

* Consider low dose of an <u>SSRI</u> (e.g., <u>escitalopram</u> or <u>citalopram</u>).

* See “<u>Depression in older adults</u>.”

* <u>Agitation</u> and <u>psychosis</u> [[31]](/library/ZwcZhe0)[[43]](/library/bfWHkk0)

* Avoid <u>antipsychotic medications</u> if possible.

* Focus on <u>delirium prevention</u> and nonpharmacological deescalation. [[43]](/library/bfWHkk0)

* If other approaches have failed or the patient poses a substantial threat to themself or others, consider one of the following:

* <u>Citalopram</u>  [[44]](/library/-wcDle0)

* Low dose of an <u>antipsychotic</u>  [[43]](/library/bfWHkk0)

* If indicated, administer under medical supervision and in a time-limited fashion.

* See “<u>Delirium management</u>” and “<u>Management of the agitated patient</u>.”

* <u>Sleep disorders</u> and disturbances [[28]](/library/-DcDSe0)

* Nonpharmacological measures are preferred, e.g.:

* <u>Sleep hygiene</u>

* Environmental restructuring

* Address possible underlying causes (e.g., drug effects, <u>nocturia</u>, <u>pain</u>).

* Consider <u>pharmacotherapy for insomnia</u> (e.g., <u>trazodone</u>) if other methods have failed and benefits are expected to outweigh the risks.

* Avoid medications that increase the risk of <u>delirium</u>, disinhibition, daytime sedation, and/or falls.





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid drugs with strong <u>anticholinergic effects</u> (e.g., <u>tricyclic antidepressants</u>, <u>diphenhydramine</u>) and use the lowest effective dose of psychoactive drugs. [[30]](/library/nDc7Ue0)




> [!WARNING]
> Only consider using <u>antipsychotics</u> to treat psychobehavioral <u>symptoms of dementia</u> if nonpharmacological measures (e.g., <u>deescalation techniques</u>) have been unsuccessful or there is concern that the patient may pose a threat to themselves or others. [[43]](/library/bfWHkk0)




### Management of conditions in advanced dementia [[3]](/library/9DcNge0)[[32]](/library/awcQhe0)




#### <u>Malnutrition</u> and weight loss [[45]](/library/I21YQT0)




* Screen for <u>malnutrition in older adults</u> every 3–6 months and monitor <u>BMI</u>.

* Assess for potential causes and initiate management accordingly.

* Ensure support to enable adequate food intake as needed.

* Avoid dietary restrictions and recommend providing food based on personal preference.

* Avoid <u>appetite stimulants</u>.

* Individualize decisions on artificial nutrition and hydration.

* Consider time-limited use of a gastrointestinal tube in patients with mild to moderate dementia.

* Provide oral feedings by hand instead of <u>tube feedings</u> in patients with severe dementia.  [[45]](/library/I21YQT0)[[46]](/library/ffWklk0)[[47]](/library/LbWw8P0)

* Withholding nutrition and hydration at the end of life is not thought to affect patient comfort. [[32]](/library/awcQhe0)





> [!WARNING]
> Do not initiate <u>tube feeding</u> in patients with severe dementia. [[34]](/library/CS1qbg0)[[45]](/library/I21YQT0)




#### Fecal and <u>urinary incontinence</u>




* Evaluate for potentially reversible causes.

* Ensure adequate hygiene to avoid <u>skin</u> breakdown and infections.

* Use pharmacotherapy with caution; <u>conservative management</u> is preferred, e.g., prompted voiding.

* See “<u>General treatment of urinary incontinence</u>.”





#### Infections




* Focus on prevention.

* Assess for <u>aspiration risk factors</u>.

* Avoid <u>indwelling urine catheters</u>.

* Monitor <u>skin</u> for <u>pressure ulcers</u>.

* Ensure antimicrobial treatment is only administered if patients meet indications.  [[48]](/library/D211PT0)

* If indicated, prescribe <u>targeted antibiotic therapy</u> in keeping with the patient's <u>goals of care</u>.
